c1.story:
Imagine Brent crude jumps by ten dollars overnight. In Dehradun, at ONGC's headquarters, someone is smiling: every barrel pumped out of Mumbai High just became worth more. In Mumbai, at the offices of BPCL and HPCL, someone is wincing: they buy that crude at the new price, but the petrol pump outside still charges yesterday's price, because nobody in Delhi has said it may change. At Jamnagar, Reliance shrugs and checks what diesel and polymer prices did, because its profit lives in the gap between crude and products, not in crude itself. And at Petronet's Dahej terminal, the reaction is roughly: so what? It gets paid a fee for every unit of gas it warms up, whatever that gas costs.

Same barrel. Four completely different reactions. That is the first thing to understand about Indian oil and gas: it is one raw material and four businesses that sit at different seats around it.

The government sits at the table too, and it is not a quiet guest. When crude spiked in 2022, it froze pump prices, which left the three oil marketing companies, or OMCs, swallowing losses on every litre, and in July of that year it slapped a windfall tax on ONGC and Oil India so they could not keep the full gain either. When crude fell, the pumps stayed frozen and the OMCs had the best year in their history. The state giveth, the state taketh, and it does both to the same companies in different years.

In Indian oil, everyone buys the same barrel. What you actually own is a seat at the table when its price moves.

Then there are the quieter names: Petronet, the trust that owns Reliance's old east-west gas pipeline, and service companies like Deep Industries and Seamec that rent out rigs, compressors and dive vessels. They are boring in the best sense. Their earnings depend on how much is handled, not on what it costs, which is precisely why the market pays up for them when nobody can agree on where crude is heading.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four doors. Read each top to bottom, then compare them side by side.

  • The name and the line under it tell you how the money is made: selling crude at a world price minus the government's cut, refining and retailing fuel at a steered price, running one giant integrated site, or charging a fee per unit moved.
  • The tickers are the listed names behind each door. Click any of them to open its stock page. Notice that MRPL and CHENNPETRO sit with the state marketers: they are refining subsidiaries of ONGC and IOC respectively, so they ride the same refining spread.
  • The bar shows how much of the profit the company gets to keep rather than hand to suppliers, customers or the state. Look at the surprise: the giant is not at the top. Upstream and Reliance sit at medium, the OMCs at low, and the small tollkeepers at high. Size is not the same thing as bargaining power.
  • The last line is the bet you are making. Read the first two together: upstream is a bet on crude rising, the OMCs a bet on crude falling while pumps stay put. They are mirror images.

The analogy below the tiles is worth a second look: the farmer, the baker whose loaf price the collector sets, the owner of everything, and the toll road. Try this test with any headline about crude. Go tile by tile and say whether it is good or bad news for that door. If your answers do not differ across the tiles, you have not read the headline closely enough.

c2.story:
Follow one barrel. It might start life in Basra, in Ras Tanura, or in a Russian Baltic port, loaded onto a tanker heading for India's west coast. India pumps less than a sixth of the crude it burns, so the overwhelming majority of the oil in your car began its journey in someone else's country, priced in someone else's currency.

The tanker docks off Gujarat, where the single buoy moorings near Jamnagar and Vadinar suck the crude ashore. LNG, gas frozen into a liquid, arrives at Petronet's Dahej terminal, gets warmed back into gas, and enters the pipeline grid. From the coast, crude pipelines run inland to refineries in the north and east, which is why those refineries carry an extra freight bill that Jamnagar never pays.

Inside a refinery the barrel is heated and split into petrol, diesel, jet fuel, LPG and naphtha. Some of the naphtha and gas goes to the petrochemicals station, where it becomes polymer granules, polyester and fertiliser feedstock. Everything else heads for the last station: the petrol pump, the LPG dealer, the city gas network. IOC, BPCL and HPCL own most of the pumps; Jio-bp and Nayara run the rest.

Here is what makes this kitchen unusual. Indian companies own almost every station from the port onwards. The squeeze does not come from a foreign rival crowding the middle, the way China crowds chemicals. It comes from the two ends: OPEC+ sets the price of the ingredient at the very first station, and the government steers the price of the dish at the very last one. The listed companies live in between, with one hand tied at each end.

India is a margin business sitting on an imported raw material.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, then the band row underneath.

The boxes are the stations, from the well to your fuel tank. Under each one you get what happens there and who stands there. Notice the shift in names: Gulf producers and ONGC at the well, Petronet and pipeline owners at the coast, Reliance and the PSU refiners in the middle, then the same PSUs again at the pump. The state marketers appear at three stations, which is why their earnings have so many moving parts.

The band row tells you who holds each station. The first band, OPEC+ and ONGC, is coloured as a rival: the price at that station is set abroad, and ONGC, though Indian, is a price taker sitting in the same box. Every band after that is coloured as India listed. Compare that with most industries on this page, where the Indian colour covers only a station or two. Here Indians own the kitchen; they just do not own the price of the ingredient.

The second band row shows where the rival stands, and here it is OPEC+ and the Gulf refiners, repeated under every station from the well to the pump. That is not a drawing quirk to skip past. OPEC+ sets the price at station one, the Gulf refiners compete at station three for the export customers Jamnagar and the coastal PSU refineries also chase, and the world price they create reaches all the way to station five, where it decides whether a frozen pump earns or bleeds.

Use the diagram to trace shocks. A sanctions headline enters at station one and lands on every refiner's crude bill. A pump-price freeze enters at station five and lands only on the marketers. A Chinese polymer glut enters at station four and lands mostly on Reliance. Ask which station a piece of news hits before you ask which stock it hits.

c3.story:
If you want to know how an Indian refiner's quarter went before it reports, do not watch crude. Watch trucks. Diesel is the biggest single product coming out of an Indian refinery, and diesel is burned mostly by lorries hauling goods along the highways. When freight is busy, diesel sells; when factories slow and trucks sit idle at the dhabas, diesel volumes wilt. A weak freight quarter shows up in OMC volumes and in the diesel crack, the gap between the diesel price and crude, before it shows up almost anywhere else.

Petrol is the two-wheeler's fuel, and it rises with commuting and new scooter sales. LPG is the household story: the Ujjwala scheme, launched in 2016, put cylinders into crores of poor kitchens, which is wonderful for public health and complicated for the OMCs, because household LPG is sold below cost and the gap is the government's promise to pay later.

Then come the customers who pay market prices. Airlines buy jet fuel, revised every month and heavily taxed by states. Fertiliser plants buy natural gas as feedstock for urea, under a pooled price the government arranges. Road builders buy bitumen, which sells briskly in the dry months and almost stops when the monsoon shuts construction. Plastics and textile makers buy polymers and the polyester chain, and they compare every Reliance price with what a Chinese cracker will offer.

Finally, export buyers. Jamnagar and the coastal PSU refineries ship diesel and jet fuel abroad, and Europe has been a prized market since its own refiners shrank. That is why the EU's ban on fuel refined from Russian crude matters here: an Indian exporter now has to prove where its crude came from or lose a premium buyer.
c3.read:
Eight tiles, one per customer group. Each tile reads in three lines.

  • The name is who is buying.
  • The second line is what they buy: diesel and petrol, LPG, jet fuel, gas, bitumen, polymers.
  • The third line is what moves that customer, which is your watch list outside the oil industry.

The most useful way to read this grid is to sort the tiles by who sets the price. Road transport and households buy at prices the government steers: petrol, diesel and LPG. Airlines, road builders, plastics makers and export buyers pay prices that move with the market every month or every day. Fertiliser plants sit in between, on a pooled, policy-arranged price.

Why does that sorting matter? Because an OMC's real profitability depends on its mix. The market-priced tiles pay whatever the world allows; the steered tiles pay whatever Delhi allows. In a year like 2026, with crude high and pumps frozen, the steered tiles are where the losses sit, and the market-priced tiles quietly carry the business.

The so-what line under the grid names diesel as the swing product. Find the road transport tile and keep it in mind for card eleven, where freight and vehicle sales show up as a one-quarter lead signal.

c4.story:
Put a state refiner and an upstream producer side by side, and their profit and loss statements barely look like they belong to the same industry.

Start with the refiner and marketer. Nearly all of its sales go straight back out the door to pay for crude. What remains has to cover the refinery's energy, staff and freight, then depreciation and interest, and what is left at the bottom is a sliver. That sliver is the whole game, and it is fragile. A few dollars on crude that the pump is not allowed to pass on, and the sliver turns into a loss. A few dollars the other way, with pumps held, and it turns into a windfall. FY24 was the windfall year; mid-2022 was the loss half-year.

Worse, the quarter you see is often not the quarter that happened. A refinery holds weeks of crude in tanks and in transit. When crude rises, that stock is suddenly worth more and the profit looks flattered; when crude falls, the same stock is marked down. Analysts call it the inventory gain or loss, and stripping it out is the first thing anyone serious does with an OMC result.

A refiner's quarter has three layers: the market's margin, the government's margin, and the tank's mood. Peel them apart before you judge it.

Now the upstream producer. It does not buy crude; it pumps it. Its biggest bite is not a supplier but the state: royalty to the states, cess to the centre, and in hot years a windfall tax. After that come the real costs of producing oil, running offshore platforms in the Arabian Sea and keeping decades-old fields alive, plus heavy depreciation, because wells deplete and must be replaced. What is left is a large slice of each rupee. The catch is that headline Brent is not what ONGC earns. It earns Brent minus discounts minus the government's cut, and the cut tends to grow exactly when Brent gets exciting.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left. Read each from left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees of sales.
  • The input bar is labelled crude and gas bought, or levies paid on it, because it means different things on each chart. For refiners and marketers it is the crude bill, and it eats nearly nine of every ten rupees. For upstream producers it is the government's cut, royalty and cess, which takes roughly a third.
  • The opex bar is energy, people and freight. It is small for the refiner and much bigger for upstream, where platforms and ageing fields cost real money to run.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is modest for the refiner and close to a fifth of sales for upstream, the price of replacing depleting wells.
  • The last bar is what is left. On the refiner's chart it is a sliver of a few rupees; on upstream's it is more than a quarter. That contrast is the whole card in one glance.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the amount. Notice how little room the refiner's last bar has: a small move in crude is a large move in profit.

Below the charts, the list marks which lines matter. Count the noes: there are none. Every line matters at least sometimes, which is unusual. Gross refining margin, marketing margin, inventory gains, capex and the government's levies all get a clear yes. Then read the so-what: strip inventory gains, and read the refining margin and the marketing margin separately, because one is a market and the other is a policy.

c5.story:
Most industries go round their cycle once a decade. Indian oil and gas has done it almost twice since 2019.

In April 2020, with the world in lockdown, an American crude contract briefly traded below zero: sellers paid buyers to take oil off their hands. Indian refineries ran at a fraction of their capacity, and the government did something telling. Instead of passing the crash to motorists, it raised fuel excise and banked the difference. Remember that move; it is the template.

Then demand roared back, Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and diesel and jet cracks hit records. Reliance and the upstream companies minted money. But Brent climbed far above a hundred dollars, and the government froze pump prices in April 2022 and imposed the windfall tax that July. The OMCs posted their worst losses in years in a single half-year, while ONGC watched the state skim its windfall. India also began buying discounted Russian crude by the tanker-load, a quiet gift to every refiner.

The flip side came fast. Crude slid into the eighties, pump prices stayed frozen, and FY24 became the best year in OMC history. A small cut arrived just before the 2024 general election. In 2025 crude fell into the sixties, the windfall tax had been scrapped, upstream earnings sagged, and America slapped an extra tariff on India over its Russian purchases.

And now the wheel is back near the top. Sanctions on Russian and Iranian barrels and the shadow fleet of tankers that carries them have pushed Brent back above a hundred. Pumps have not moved. So the OMCs are losing on diesel again, and ONGC and Oil India are enjoying their best realisation in years.

In this industry the cycle has two faces. Every boom for the well is a bust for the pump.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, running clockwise from the top. The years under each arc come from the last full lap: boom in 2021 and 2022, peak in 2022, bust through 2023 and 2024, bottom in 2025. The arrow points to today, and for oil and gas it sits in the middle of the peak arc, on the lower right, labelled a crude spike on sanctions. One caution: the clock is drawn through the crude price, so it reads naturally for upstream. For the OMCs, a crude peak is their trough. The phase notes say so: the peak is when the OMCs post their worst losses.

The timeline beside it runs year by year from 2019. Watch the colours alternate: the 2020 entry is a bust, 2021 and 2022 a boom, FY24 another boom (for the OMCs), 2025 a bust (for upstream), and 2026 is marked now. The alternation is the two-faced cycle drawn in colour.

The four hands let you move the arrow yourself.

  • Brent crude: above a hundred, pointing up. Good for upstream, painful for the pump.
  • Singapore refining margin: firm, pointing up. Every refiner earns more per barrel, whatever the pump policy.
  • OMC marketing margin on diesel: negative, pointing down. The day it turns positive without a price hike, crude has fallen enough to rescue the marketers.
  • Russian crude discount and sanctions: narrowing, a mixed reading. The cheap barrel is getting less cheap.

The so-what under the hands is the trading instruction: upstream first, OMCs last, and be ready to flip the day Brent breaks.

c6.story:
An Indian oil company's results are decided in rooms its managers never enter. In Riyadh and Vienna, OPEC+ ministers decide how much crude to hold back. In Washington, the Treasury decides which tankers and which Russian sellers to sanction. In Singapore, traders price diesel and jet fuel every day. And in Shastri Bhawan in Delhi, the petroleum ministry decides, without ever writing it down, whether the pump price is allowed to move.

Three dials carry the heaviest weight. Brent is the obvious one, but it is two-faced: a rise lifts ONGC and Oil India and squeezes the OMCs. The Singapore refining margin is the clean one: when the gap between crude and Asian product prices widens, every refiner from Jamnagar to Kochi earns more per barrel. The third is pump-price policy, and it is the dial the market most often underrates. A single hike restores OMC margins overnight; a freeze before an election can cost them a quarter's profit.

Then come the two-dot dials. A weaker rupee raises the import bill, because every barrel is bought in dollars and sold at the pump in rupees. Sanctions on Russian and Iranian oil decide whether Indian refiners keep a discount on a big chunk of their crude. Spot LNG decides whether fertiliser and power plants burn imported gas or switch to something else, which shows up in Petronet's volumes. Windfall levies cap what upstream keeps of any rally. And Chinese petrochemical exports set the ceiling on Reliance's polymer spread.

Last, the slow dials. Domestic fuel demand grows steadily. Ethanol blending, which reached the twenty per cent target ahead of the original schedule, and electric two-wheelers chip away at petrol, a little every year, never dramatically in any one quarter.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force, from Brent to electric vehicles.
  • Channel: how it reaches profits. For Brent the channel cell is long, because it hits upstream realisation, refiners' input cost and inventory, and marketing margins all at once.
  • A rise does: a green up arrow means a rise helps the industry, a red down arrow means it hurts, and a diamond means it depends on the door. Brent carries a diamond for exactly that reason.
  • Weight: one to three dots. Three dots can make or break a year.

Scan the three-dot rows first: Brent, the Singapore margin and pump-price policy. Two of the three are about the refiner's spread; that tells you where the volatility in this industry lives.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track. Brent and the rupee are direct. Some others are honest proxies: the Singapore margin row shows the core-sector refinery output index, the pump-policy row shows transport inflation, the spot LNG row shows domestic gas output, and the electric-vehicle row shows the auto index. Read those as the nearest weather station, not the exact reading. Rows with a dash, like sanctions or windfall levies, have no series; you follow those in the news.

Then count the red arrows: rupee, sanctions, LNG, levies, Chinese petchem, transition. Most outside forces hurt this industry when they rise, which is why the so-what tells you to track just Brent and the Singapore margin and let the rest confirm.

c7.story:
Why do the three state OMCs, owners of most of India's petrol pumps and a large share of its refining, so often trade at a discount to the market? The bottleneck table answers that in eight rows, and the first three do most of the work.

Start with import dependence. India imports more than four-fifths of its crude and about half its gas. Every geopolitical shock, a war in the Gulf, a sanctions package, a pirate attack in the Red Sea, lands on the rupee, the current account and the refiners' crude bill in one go. No management team can fix that.

Then the government's hand on the pump. Petrol was freed from price control in 2010 and diesel in 2014, and daily price revision began in 2017. On paper, pump prices are market-linked. In practice, they freeze before elections and whenever crude spikes, and the OMCs carry the loss until a bailout or a crude fall rescues them. The same reflex works upstream: when crude rallies, a windfall tax appears, as it did in 2022, and disappears when crude falls, as it did at the end of 2024.

The oil marketers were deregulated by law and re-regulated by habit.

Next, ageing fields. Mumbai High was discovered in 1974. ONGC now spends heavily just to keep production flat, and big new discoveries have been rare despite repeated rounds of open acreage auctions. LPG under-recoveries are another recurring drain: cylinders sold below cost, compensation late and partial.

The live swing factor is sanctions. India's purchases of discounted Russian crude were a windfall for refiners after 2022. Now sanctions, tariffs and tanker insurance decide each quarter whether that discount survives. Further out sit the Chinese petrochemical glut and the slow march of ethanol and electric vehicles.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity label. The label tells you where the risk belongs in your thinking.

  • Structural: import dependence and ageing fields. These never go away; they belong in the valuation multiple, not in a news alert.
  • Recurring: the pump freeze, the windfall-tax reflex and LPG under-recoveries. Notice that all three are made by the government. Together they are one cluster, policy risk, and it is the main reason OMCs trade cheaply and upstream rarely gets full credit for a crude rally.
  • Two-sided: sanctions and shipping. Sanctions created the Russian discount that helped refiners, and tighter sanctions can take it away. The same row can be a tailwind one year and a headwind the next.
  • Cyclical: the Chinese petchem glut. It bites for years at a time and then eases, mostly a Reliance question.
  • Slow: the energy transition. Real, but measured in years, not quarters.

Read the so-what line with the table in front of you: the first three rows are the permanent shape of the sector, and the sanctions row is the one worth a daily look this year. If you own an OMC, map each recurring row to a question for the next results call: how big are the LPG dues, what is the diesel marketing loss, and has anything been said about pump prices?

c8.story:
In most industries the regulator sets the rules and the market sets the price. In Indian oil, the regulator and the owner are often the same people, and the price is set somewhere in between, in conversations that leave no paper trail.

The petroleum ministry owns the PSUs and steers pump prices without a written rule. There is no notification announcing a freeze; prices simply stop moving, and the OMCs absorb the difference. The finance ministry is the other hand on the lever. When crude crashed in 2020, the centre raised excise and kept the gain. On the eve of Diwali in 2021, it cut excise to share relief with motorists. Excise and state VAT together make up a large part of what you pay at the pump, so a tax change is often how crude relief reaches you, or does not.

Upstream has its own rulebook. The Directorate General of Hydrocarbons auctions exploration blocks under the open acreage policy, where explorers pick their own areas and bid. The new Oilfields Amendment Act separates petroleum from mining law and lengthens leases, an attempt to make India attractive to foreign explorers who have mostly stayed away. Gas from old fields is priced by a formula, set in 2023, at a slice of the crude price with a floor and a ceiling, which decides both ONGC's gas income and the input cost of city gas and fertiliser.

And then the levy that hangs over every rally. The windfall tax, imposed in 2022 and scrapped at the end of 2024, is gone but not forgotten. With Brent back above a hundred, it is the first thing anyone owning ONGC reads in a budget speech. From outside, the EU's ban on fuel made from Russian crude adds a new compliance test for Indian exporters.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule: who it is, what it does, why you care, and a status tag.

  • Always: the ministry, the hydrocarbons directorate, the gas regulator PNGRB, fuel excise and VAT, and the safety and environment clearances. These are the permanent fixtures. Note that the ministry's row says it steers prices without a written rule; that one line explains half the OMC discount.
  • Live: the domestic gas pricing formula and the windfall tax. The windfall tax is marked live even though it was scrapped, because the conditions that triggered it, crude far above a hundred, are back. Treat it as a loaded rule, not a dead one.
  • New: the Oilfields Amendment Act and the EU ban on fuel refined from Russian crude. The first is a slow tailwind for upstream; the second is an immediate test for exporters' crude slates.

A practical way to use the table: for each door, find the rows that touch it. Upstream lives under the hydrocarbons directorate, the gas formula and the windfall tax. The OMCs live under the ministry and excise. Petronet and the pipeline trust live under PNGRB. Reliance touches almost every row, plus the EU ban on its export barrels.

Dated regulatory news filtered for this industry sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces ask one blunt question: once money comes into the industry, who walks away with it? Run the OMCs through it and you find a genuine puzzle.

Rivalry is low. Three state companies own most of the pumps, and they price identically, almost to the paisa. New entrants are rare: a refinery costs tens of thousands of crore, and a network of pumps takes decades to build. By the textbook, this should be a fat, comfortable oligopoly. So why do the OMCs keep so little?

Two spokes. On the supplier side, they buy crude from OPEC+ and from sanctioned sellers at whatever the world charges; there is no negotiating with Riyadh. On the buyer side, the real buyer is not the motorist. It is the government, which decides what the motorist pays. A company whose largest customer is also its regulator and its majority shareholder does not have much bargaining power with anyone.

The OMCs' problem was never competition. It is that their customer, their regulator and their owner share an office.

Now the other shape: upstream and the tollkeepers. Upstream's supplier is geology, which does not send invoices. The tollkeepers' customers sign long take-or-pay contracts, paying for the agreed volume whether or not they use it, which is why Petronet's earnings are so steady. Substitutes barely bite: nothing replaces crude in petrochemicals soon, and nothing replaces a pipeline except not moving gas. The one spoke where this shape reaches out is buyer power, because gas buyers do switch to coal or propane when spot LNG is dear, and because the government takes its cut from upstream when crude gets exciting.

Substitutes for the OMCs are real but slow: ethanol, electric scooters and gas are nibbling at petrol and diesel, a little each year.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force, starting with rivalry at the top and running clockwise through supplier power, buyer power, new entrants and substitutes. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force applies. Smaller shape, better business.

Two shapes are drawn: refiners and marketers, and upstream with the tollkeepers. Look first at the overall size. The refiners' shape is lopsided: tiny at the top and bottom left, rivalry and entrants both scored one, then shooting out to the full three on supplier and buyer power. That kite shape, pulled hard to the right, is the picture of the puzzle in the story: a cosy market squeezed from both ends.

The upstream and tollkeeper shape is compact, mostly ones, with a modest bulge on buyer power at two. Rivalry, entrants and substitutes are low for both shapes, so the shapes almost overlap on the left side. All the difference is on the right.

Substitutes sit at two for the refiners and one for the other shape: ethanol and electric vehicles nibble at fuel, while pipelines and crude for petrochemicals have no ready replacement.

The table next to the chart gives each score from zero to three and the reason. If you own a specific company, redraw its shape in your head. Reliance, for instance, is not on this chart as a separate door; it would sit between the two, with refiners' supplier pressure but far more freedom on the buyer spoke, since its pumps and exports are priced by the market.

c10.story:
An oil results day can bury you in jargon: throughput, slate, cracks, under-recoveries, realisation. Eight numbers cut through it, and the trick is knowing which ones belong to which door.

For a refiner, start with the gross refining margin, the dollars earned per barrel between crude in and products out. Compare it with the Singapore benchmark. Reliance, with its complex Jamnagar site, should beat the benchmark comfortably; the PSUs should at least keep up. Then the marketing margin per litre of diesel and petrol, which tells you whether the pump is subsidising the public or quietly minting money. Next, strip the inventory gain out of the EBITDA margin, because a crude rally flatters the reported number and a crude fall punishes it.

For upstream, the number is net crude realisation: what ONGC and Oil India actually keep per barrel after discounts and levies. If it tracks Brent closely, fine. If the gap suddenly widens, a new levy has arrived. Then production volumes, oil and gas separately, because for an ageing field portfolio, standing still is an achievement and a steady fall is a story of decline.

For the balance sheet, debt to EBITDA tells you how much of the capex and the unpaid LPG dues sit on borrowed money, and capex to depreciation tells you whether a company is building its next cracker or field or merely maintaining what it has. For the tollkeepers, the one number is utilisation: is the Dahej terminal running near full, or has spot LNG got too dear for Indian buyers?

Read the right numbers for the right door and a results day takes ten minutes, not an afternoon.
c10.read:
One row per number: what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median from filings.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask. Notice how many rows are door-specific: refining margin and marketing margin for the OMCs, net realisation and production for upstream, utilisation for the tollkeepers.
  • What good looks like carries the rules of thumb: refining margins above eight dollars a barrel for Reliance and above six for the PSUs, a marketing margin of three to five rupees a litre in a normal year, upstream realisation within a few dollars of Brent, terminal utilisation above nine-tenths at Dahej. These are benchmarks for a typical year, not targets.
  • Today's industry median comes from the listed companies' latest annual filings.

Two cautions for this industry. First, the top four rows will show a dash. Refining margin, marketing margin, realisation and production are disclosed in company presentations and ministry data, not in a standard filing line, so we cannot compute a median. Second, the medians that do appear, for EBITDA margin, debt, capex and the last row, blend four very different doors. A refiner's single-digit margin and Petronet's sixty-plus sit in the same pool, so the median is a rough centre, not a benchmark for any one company. The last row's median is an asset-turn figure standing in for utilisation.

So use the good-looks-like column door by door, and treat the median as context.

c11.story:
Oil is a fast industry. In chemicals or power, the warning signs often arrive two or three quarters before the results. Here, much of the news hits the same quarter. Brent and the Dubai benchmark move inventory gains and upstream realisations in real time. Singapore product cracks, published every week, are a near-live read on the refining margin. By the time a refiner reports, a careful reader already knows roughly what the number will be.

The earlier voices are fewer but worth hearing. OPEC+ output decisions and the count of American shale rigs are crude prices next quarter. Sanctions news on Russia, Iran and the shadow fleet decides a quarter ahead whether the discount on a big share of India's crude survives. The election calendar is the most Indian lead indicator of all: pumps freeze before polls and sometimes thaw after, so a heavy state election season is a warning for OMC margins. Asian spot LNG decides whether fertiliser and power plants keep buying imported gas. Freight and vehicle sales foreshadow diesel and petrol volumes. Only one signal speaks two quarters ahead: new Chinese crackers coming online, which set Reliance's petchem spread.

Put the pieces together and you get the rule. The OMC up-cycle starts when crude is falling, pump prices are holding and Singapore margins are firm. Two of those are ticking today: pumps are frozen and margins are firm. But the missing sign, crude falling, is the master switch. With crude rising, a frozen pump is not a cushion, it is a leak, and losses pile up. Flip one sign, crude breaking lower, and the very same frozen pumps become a windfall. For upstream, read the first sign the other way round: crude rising is the tick it wants.

That is why the call leans to upstream and the tollkeepers, with a finger on the switch.

The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for the channel through which it reaches earnings.

Look at the shape of the dots before reading any one of them. They crowd the left and the middle: Brent and Singapore cracks at the same quarter; OPEC+, sanctions, the election calendar, spot LNG and freight one quarter ahead. Only the Chinese cracker dot sits further right, at two quarters. The lesson is that oil gives little early warning. Your edge here comes from reacting quickly and reading the same-quarter signals properly, not from forecasting far ahead.

Below the chart sits the rule with three signs. Crude falling has a cross, with the note that it is above a hundred and rising. Pump prices holding has a tick, but read its note: frozen, so losses pile up. Singapore margins firm has a tick. Two ticks out of three would normally read as early recovery, but this is the case where you weigh the signs, not count them: the cross is on the one sign that turns the other two from pain into profit.

The call box then gives the headline, the three points behind it, and the list of what would change it: sanctions relief or an OPEC+ output rise taking Brent back toward the seventies, the windfall tax returning, or a pump hike or excise cut. Set those three as news alerts. Any one of them is a reason to revisit which door you prefer.
